name: The Dog: First Domesticate
scope: The gray wolf (Canis lupus) as ancestor of every dog; the ~15,000-40,000 BP domestication window (oldest of all); the single-vs-multiple-origin debate; the human-camp scavenging pathway; how commensal wolves diverged behaviorally before morphologically; the Bonn-Oberkassel dog burial (~14,000 BP) as early companionship evidence.
source: Britannica; Larson & Bradley (2014, PLOS Genetics) dog-origins review; Freedman & Wayne genome studies; Bonn-Oberkassel burial
framing_note: Scene-led: a wolf drawn to the warmth of a human fire, not 'what animal did dogs descend from?'. Practical anchor: this is the ur-story of husbandry the harvester should know. Present single-vs-multiple-origin as a live scientific debate, not a settled verdict.

name: Sheep & Goat: Fertile Crescent Firsts
scope: ~11,000 BP domestication in the Fertile Crescent; mouflon (Ovis) → sheep and bezoar ibex (Capra) → goat; among the very first agricultural domesticates alongside grain; the shift from hunting to herding; the secondary-products revolution (wool/milk after meat); why goats browse and sheep graze.
source: Britannica; Zeder domestication archaeology; The Livestock Conservancy
framing_note: Scene-led: the first herders of the Zagros foothills, wild mouflon in the hills. Concrete wild-ancestor names beat 'first livestock'. No policy drift.

name: Cattle: Aurochs to Three Origins
scope: ~10,500 BP; wild aurochs (Bos primigenius) as ancestor; independent taurine (Near East, Bos taurus) and zebu (Indian subcontinent, Bos indicus) domestications plus a distinct African line; the aurochs' 1627 extinction (last cow in Poland's Jaktorow Forest); humped vs. humpless split; the small founding herd (~80 females, genetics suggest).
source: Britannica; Zeder; Bollongino (2012) cattle-founder genetics; aurochs extinction record (Jaktorow 1627)
framing_note: Scene-led: the towering wild aurochs behind every modern cow, extinct in a Polish royal forest. Named ancestor and place beat generic 'origin'. No policy drift.

name: Pig: The Independent Boar
scope: ~9,000 BP; from wild boar (Sus scrofa); independent domestication in Anatolia AND East Asia; genetics show ongoing back-crossing with wild boar; fast reproduction and omnivory made the pig an efficient converter of scraps; the pig's taboo status in some cultures vs. its centrality in others.
source: Britannica; Larson pig-genome studies; Zeder
framing_note: Scene-led: the tusked wild boar of Anatolian oak woods. Twin-origin (Anatolia + East Asia) is the memorable fact. No policy drift.

name: The Cat Who Moved In
scope: ~9,500 BP Cyprus burial (cat interred with a human) and ~7,500 BP Egypt; from the Near Eastern wildcat (Felis silvestris lybica); the self-domestication / commensal pathway — cats drawn to rodents in stored grain; tamer-than-tame vs. truly domesticated debate; why cats domesticated themselves late and lightly.
source: Britannica; Vigne (2004) Cyprus cat burial; Driscoll (2007) wildcat genetics
framing_note: Scene-led: a wildcat slipping into the first grain stores, then a cat buried beside its person on Cyprus. Self-domestication is the wonder beat. No policy drift.

name: The Horse: Botai Revolution
scope: ~5,500 BP Botai culture, Kazakhstan (bit wear on teeth, mare's-milk residue in pots); how the horse transformed transport, trade and warfare; the later discovery that Botai horses were Przewalski ancestors, not the source of modern domestic horses (2018 genetics twist); the true modern-horse origin traced to the Western Steppe (~4,200 BP).
source: Outram (2009) Botai study; Gaunitz (2018, Science) Przewalski reassignment; Librado (2021, Nature) horse-origins; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: milk-residue pots and bit-worn teeth on the Kazakh steppe. The 2018/2021 twists (Botai not the modern ancestor; true origin on the Western Steppe) are memorable upper-tier reveals. Present as evolving science. No policy drift.

name: Chicken: From Red Junglefowl
scope: From red junglefowl (Gallus gallus) of Southeast Asia; spread via trade; ~30 billion alive today (most numerous bird on Earth); recent evidence narrows domestication to rice-farming Southeast Asia ~3,500 years ago (revising older 5,500 BP dates); egg-then-meat use history; the rooster in myth/timekeeping.
source: Britannica; Peters (2022, PNAS) chicken-origins revision; FAO livestock counts
framing_note: Scene-led: the wild red junglefowl crowing in a Thai forest, ancestor of 30 billion birds. Named ancestor and the staggering count are the hooks. No policy drift.

name: Diamond's 14 & Why So Few
scope: Jared Diamond's list of 14 major large-herbivore domesticates and his six criteria for why so few species qualify (diet, growth rate, breeding in captivity, disposition, panic tendency, social hierarchy); why zebras, hippos, deer and bison largely failed; the geographic accident that gave Eurasia most of the winners.
source: Jared Diamond, Guns Germs and Steel; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: the biting zebra that could never be tamed vs. the biddable ox. Diamond's criteria are the reveal. No policy drift.

name: Late & Regional Domesticates
scope: The reindeer as the most recent large-animal domesticate (~2,000 BP, Siberian Sami and others, half-wild herding); the llama and alpaca (Andean, from guanaco and vicuna, ~5,000 BP, cargo + fiber); the water buffalo, yak, bactrian camel and dromedary as regional workhorses; the guinea pig and turkey as New World domesticates.
source: Britannica; FAO domestic-animal-diversity; Andean camelid domestication literature
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the most recent large-animal domesticate, still half-wild on the Siberian tundra' → reindeer; 'the Andean cargo animal bred from the wild guanaco' → llama. Named animal + region. No policy drift.

name: The Honeybee & the Egyptian Hive
scope: ~6,000 BP managed hives in Egyptian hieroglyphics (bee as symbol of Lower Egypt); honey, beeswax, propolis and royal jelly as products; Apis mellifera as a 'semi-domesticate'; sun-temple apiaries and honey as offering/currency; the queen/worker/drone caste system a keeper manages.
source: Britannica; Crane, The World History of Beekeeping; Egyptian apiary reliefs
framing_note: Scene-led: Nyuserre's sun-temple relief of Egyptians blowing smoke into pipe hives. Products (wax, propolis) beyond honey are the depth. No policy drift.

name: Angus: The Black Polled Scot
scope: Aberdeen Angus (Scotland; solid black; naturally polled/hornless; most popular US beef breed; the 'Certified Angus Beef' brand and its grading spec); why the polled gene matters for handling and dehorning; the marbling reputation; Red Angus as the recessive-color offshoot.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; American Angus Association; Certified Angus Beef; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the black, hornless Scottish breed behind most American beef' → Angus. Named breed + trait (polled, black), never 'what is a beef breed?'. No policy drift.

name: Hereford & British Beef Breeds
scope: Hereford (Herefordshire England; red body with unmistakable white face; hardy foundational ranching breed; the 'baldy' F1 cross with Angus); Shorthorn (dual-purpose, one of the earliest improved breeds, Bakewell-era selection); Devon and Galloway as hardy British beef stock.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; American Hereford Association; Britannica; Robert Bakewell breeding history
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the red breed with the white face, foundation of range ranching' → Hereford. Named breed + white-face trait. No policy drift.

name: Jersey & Channel-Island Dairy
scope: Jersey (small fawn-colored Channel Islands breed; highest butterfat in milk; gentle temperament; efficient feed-to-milk on smaller frame); Guernsey (larger, golden 'Golden Guernsey' milk high in beta-carotene); why butterfat drives cheese and cream yield; the island herd-book purity laws.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; American Jersey Cattle Association; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the small fawn Channel Islands cow whose milk carries the highest butterfat' → Jersey. Named breed + butterfat trait, never a bare definition. No policy drift.

name: Holstein: The Milk Champion
scope: Holstein-Friesian (black-and-white from Friesland/Holland; the dairy volume champion at ~10,000+ gal/cow/year; ~90% of US dairy cattle); the unique black-and-white spotting used as ID; why sheer volume (not richness) made it the industrial dairy standard; the red-and-white recessive variant.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; Holstein Association USA; USDA dairy statistics; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the black-and-white Friesian, the world's milk champion' → Holstein. Named breed + the volume record. No policy drift.

name: Wagyu, Kobe & Marbling
scope: Wagyu = the Japanese breed group (literally 'Japanese cattle'), Kobe = a protected brand of Tajima-strain Wagyu from Hyogo Prefecture only; intramuscular fat marbling (the BMS score 1-12); the four Wagyu strains (Japanese Black dominant); why 'Kobe beef' outside Hyogo is usually mislabeled; monounsaturated-fat melting point.
source: Britannica; Kobe Beef Marketing & Distribution Promotion Association; Japan Meat Grading Association
framing_note: Scene-led: the marbled Tajima steer of Hyogo. The Wagyu-is-the-breed / Kobe-is-the-brand distinction is the load-bearing reveal. No policy drift.

name: Heat-Tolerant Cattle: Brahman & Zebu
scope: Brahman (American breed from Indian zebu stock; pronounced hump, loose dewlap and sheath; heat-, humidity- and tick-tolerant; backbone of Gulf-coast ranching); the zebu (Bos indicus) genetics behind heat tolerance (extra sweat glands, sheddable coat); Santa Gertrudis and Brangus as Brahman crosses.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; American Brahman Breeders Association; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the humped, floppy-dewlapped breed that shrugs off Gulf-coast heat' → Brahman. Trait-anchored (hump, dewlap, heat tolerance). No policy drift.

name: Heritage & Continental Cattle
scope: Texas Longhorn (Spanish Andalusian descent; near-extinct ~1900 then restored; sweeping horns to ~7 ft tip-to-tip; drought-hardy); Charolais (French; white; muscular terminal sire); Highland (shaggy Scottish, long horns, hardy); Belgian Blue (double-muscling myostatin mutation); Chianina (Italian, the tallest breed).
source: The Livestock Conservancy; Britannica; breed associations
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the sweeping-horned survivors of the Spanish herds' → Texas Longhorn; 'the double-muscled Belgian breed with a myostatin mutation' → Belgian Blue. Named breed + signature trait. No policy drift.

name: Artificial Insemination & Cattle Genetics
scope: First commercial AI 1936-38 (USDA / cooperative bull studs); the frozen-semen revolution (liquid-nitrogen straws, 1950s); the estrus cycle and heat detection; how a single elite bull can now sire millions of calves; sexed semen for dairy-heifer selection; genetics acceleration vs. gene-pool narrowing.
source: USDA history of AI; Foote (2002) 'The history of artificial insemination'; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: the first cooperative bull stud and the leap to frozen straws. Concrete milestone (1936-38) constructed by the stem. Note gene-pool narrowing neutrally; no policy drift.

name: Milk Across Species
scope: Cow, goat, sheep, water buffalo (Indian dairy backbone + mozzarella di bufala), yak (Himalayan), camel, horse (mare's-milk airag/kumis) and reindeer all milked; goat milk's smaller fat globules (easier digestion, pH nearer human milk); sheep milk highest fat (~7% vs. cow ~3.5%, base of Roquefort/Pecorino/feta); camel milk's lower lactose and insulin-like protein researched for diabetics.
source: Britannica; FAO dairy species data; Park (2007) minor-species milk composition
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the milk with the highest fat, curdled into Roquefort' → sheep; 'the low-lactose desert milk researched for diabetics' → camel. Named cheeses and species are the handles. Camel-milk diabetic claim framed as researched, not proven. No policy drift.

name: A2 vs. A1 Milk Debate
scope: A1 and A2 beta-casein variants differ by one amino acid (histidine vs. proline at position 67); A2 proponents claim easier digestion and fewer symptoms (BCM-7 peptide hypothesis); the a2 Milk Company marketing; mainstream reviews find no convincing evidence A1 harms most people while some gut-microbiota studies show differences; the between-country-correlation critique.
source: Truswell (2005) 'The A2 milk case: a critical review'; MDPI 2025 human-studies review; a2 Milk Company
framing_note: CONTESTED — both sides, no verdict. Attribute the digestion/BCM-7 claim to proponents; attribute the null finding to the mainstream reviews; let choices be competing positions. Scene-led on the single-amino-acid difference. No policy drift.

name: From Milk to Cheese & Butter
scope: Rennet (chymosin) curdling milk into curds and whey; the butterfat-to-butter churning; cream separation; why buffalo/sheep milk suits mozzarella/feta; lactose and the lactase-persistence mutation that let dairying spread; raw-milk vs. pasteurized tradeoffs; ghee and yogurt as preservation.
source: Britannica; McGee, On Food and Cooking (dairy chapter); lactase-persistence genetics literature
framing_note: Scene-led + practical (harvest-relevant dairy processing): 'the enzyme from a calf's stomach that splits milk into curds and whey' → rennet. The lactase-persistence mutation is the wonder beat (a gene that rewrote diets). No policy drift.

name: Water Buffalo & Dairy Buffalo
scope: The domestic water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis) - the river type (India/Italy, Murrah and Mediterranea breeds, dairy) vs. the swamp type (Southeast Asia, draft/paddy work); mozzarella di bufala DOP from Italian Mediterranea buffalo; buffalo milk's high fat and solids; the buffalo as the backbone of Indian dairy (the world's largest milk producer).
source: FAO; Britannica; Consorzio Mozzarella di Bufala Campana DOP
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the buffalo milk curdled into DOP mozzarella in Campania' -> Mediterranea/river buffalo. River-vs-swamp type split is the reveal. No policy drift.

name: Milking: By Hand to Rotary Parlor
scope: Hand-milking and the letdown reflex (oxytocin); the vacuum milking machine (patented late 1800s) that ended hand-milking at scale; the herringbone and rotary carousel parlors; robotic voluntary milking systems where the cow chooses when to be milked; twice-daily vs. thrice-daily; teat health and mastitis prevention.
source: Britannica; dairy-technology histories; De Laval milking-machine history
framing_note: Scene-led: the rotary carousel turning cows past a single operator, or the robot the cow visits on her own schedule. Named milestone (vacuum machine) + the letdown reflex. No policy drift.

name: Merino & the Fine-Wool Story
scope: Merino (Spanish origin, once a Crown monopoly with live export banned on pain of death; Australian dominance today; finest wool at ~17-22 micrometers); crimp and staple length; superfine merino for next-to-skin garments; the annual wool clip and shearing; why fiber diameter defines value and 'itch'.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; Britannica; Australian Wool Innovation
framing_note: Scene-led: the Spanish Crown guarding its Merino flocks, then the great Australian wool clip. Fiber diameter (microns) is the number the stem constructs. No policy drift.

name: Meat & Dual-Purpose Sheep
scope: Suffolk (English; black face and legs, white body; dominant terminal meat sire); Dorset (English; out-of-season breeder; milk+meat+wool); Hampshire, Texel (heavily muscled) and Southdown as meat breeds; the terminal-sire concept; Katahdin/hair sheep that shed and need no shearing.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; Britannica; National Sheep Association (UK)
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the black-faced English breed that sires most market lambs' → Suffolk; 'the breed that will lamb out of season' → Dorset. Trait-anchored, never 'name a meat sheep'. No policy drift.

name: Wool Grades & Specialty Fibers
scope: Wool grades by micrometer (superfine <18µm → fine → medium → strong/carpet); the micron count as the price driver; specialty animal fibers — cashmere (goat undercoat), mohair (Angora goat), angora (rabbit), alpaca, qiviut (muskox, warmest fiber); lanolin as a wool byproduct.
source: Britannica; The Livestock Conservancy; textile-fiber references
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the warmest natural fiber, combed from the muskox undercoat' → qiviut; 'the fiber from the Angora goat' → mohair. Named fiber + source animal (note angora=rabbit vs. Angora goat=mohair, the classic trap). No policy drift.

name: Karakul & Persian Lamb Fur
scope: Karakul (Central Asian fat-tailed sheep, one of the oldest domesticated breeds); Persian lamb / astrakhan / broadtail fur taken from newborn or unborn lambs for the tight lustrous curl; the practice's history in Bukhara/Afghanistan and the welfare controversy over slaughtering neonates and pregnant ewes.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; Britannica 'astrakhan'; welfare-critic sources
framing_note: CONTESTED practice — note it explicitly and even-handedly: state the tight-curl fur trade and the neonate/unborn-lamb welfare objection side by side, no verdict. Scene-led on the fat-tailed steppe sheep. No policy drift.

name: Goat Breeds: Dairy, Meat & Fiber
scope: Nubian (long floppy ears, high-butterfat milk), Alpine and Saanen (the white Swiss 'Holstein of goats', top dairy volume), Nigerian Dwarf (tiny, rich milk); Boer (South African, the premier meat goat, red head); Angora (mohair) and Cashmere goats; the browsing habit that clears brush; fainting (myotonic) goats.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; American Dairy Goat Association; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the long-eared breed whose milk carries the highest butterfat' -> Nubian; 'the red-headed South African meat goat' -> Boer. Named breed + trait, never 'name a goat'. No policy drift.

name: Shearing & Wool Harvest
scope: The annual shearing (a skilled shearer can do a sheep in ~2 minutes; Australian blade-vs-machine records); why most sheep must be shorn (they no longer shed like their wild ancestors); the fleece skirted and graded; 'wigging' and crutching for hygiene; the New Zealand/Australian shearing-shed culture; mulesing as a contested flystrike-prevention practice.
source: Britannica; Australian Wool Innovation; shearing-record histories
framing_note: Scene-led: the champion shearer clearing a full fleece in a couple of minutes. Note mulesing even-handedly as a contested welfare practice (flystrike prevention vs. pain objection), no verdict. Practical harvest anchor. No policy drift.

name: Yorkshire, Landrace & Commercial Pork
scope: Large White / Yorkshire (English; white; lean; prolific — the genetic backbone of most commercial pork); Landrace (long-bodied Danish, extra rib, bacon length); Duroc (red American, marbling terminal sire); Hampshire (black with a white belt); the three-way commercial cross and why hybrid vigor drives production.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; Britannica; National Pig Association (UK); National Swine Registry
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the lean white English pig behind most commercial pork' → Yorkshire; 'the long Danish breed bred for an extra rib and bacon length' → Landrace. Named breed + trait. No policy drift.

name: Heritage & Acorn-Fed Pigs
scope: Berkshire (English heritage, black with six white points, prized 'Kurobuta' pork); Tamworth (Irish/English, ginger-red, the classic bacon pig); Iberico of the Spanish dehesa (Pata Negra; Bellota grade acorn-finished for jamon iberico); Mangalitsa (Hungarian curly 'wooly pig', near-extinct then restored, extreme lard marbling); Gloucestershire Old Spots; why acorn/pannage finishing changes the fat.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; Britannica; Fundacion del Jamon Iberico; Mangalica breeders
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the curly-coated Hungarian wooly pig' → Mangalitsa; 'the black-hoofed pig fattened on dehesa acorns for jamon' → Iberico. Acorn-finishing is the memorable practical hook (fat quality). No policy drift.

name: Pig Husbandry & Gestation Housing
scope: The sow's reproductive cycle and large litters; the farrowing crate and the welfare debate over gestation stalls vs. group housing (piglet-crushing safety vs. sow confinement); weaning age; the pig's intelligence and rooting instinct; enrichment and why bored pigs tail-bite; the shift among producers toward crate-free systems.
source: Britannica; welfare-science literature on sow housing; National Pork Board
framing_note: CONTESTED within a firm floor: the piglet-crushing safety rationale for crates is real AND the sow-confinement welfare cost is real - present the crate-vs-group-housing tradeoff as a genuine debate, no verdict; note the intelligent, rooting pig deserving enrichment as the firm humane thread. Scene-led. No legislative/policy drift.

name: Chicken Layers & Broilers
scope: Leghorn (Italian; white feathers and white eggs; the dominant commercial layer); Rhode Island Red (American, 1854; dual-purpose; brown eggs); Plymouth Rock (American, 1869; barred plumage; dual-purpose); Cornish (English; the broiler foundation crossed to make the Cornish Cross meat bird); Sussex and Orpington as dual-purpose heritage; layer-vs-broiler divergence.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; American Poultry Association Standard of Perfection; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the white Italian hen laying most of the world's white eggs' → Leghorn; 'the English breed crossed to build the meat broiler' → Cornish. Named breed + product. No policy drift.

name: Ornamental Fowl & Egg-Color Genetics
scope: Silkie (Chinese; fluffy hair-like plumage; black skin and bones; five toes where most chickens have four; blue earlobes); Ameraucana/Araucana blue eggs; the earlobe-color rule of thumb (white earlobes → white eggs, red → brown) and its exceptions; egg-shell pigment (protoporphyrin brown, oocyanin blue) laid down in the shell gland; the Marans' chocolate-brown egg.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; American Poultry Association; egg-pigment genetics literature
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the fluffy black-skinned five-toed Chinese fowl' → Silkie; earlobe-color as the surprising predictor of egg color. Wonder over rote. No policy drift.

name: Ducks, Geese & Turkeys
scope: Pekin duck (white; dominant meat duck; from China via Long Island); Muscovy (the only domestic duck not descended from mallard); Toulouse and Embden geese; the Broad-Breasted White and Bronze turkeys vs. heritage Bourbon Red / Narragansett / Standard Bronze; why the industrial turkey can no longer breed naturally (AI required); foie gras from Moulard ducks (note the controversy).
source: The Livestock Conservancy; Britannica; American Poultry Association
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the white Long Island duck on every Peking-duck menu' → Pekin; 'the only domestic duck not from the mallard' → Muscovy. Note foie gras and the AI-only industrial turkey as contested/telling facts even-handedly, no verdict. No policy drift.

name: Incubation & Hatchery Craft
scope: The 21-day chicken incubation; candling to check fertility and development; egg-turning and humidity in the incubator; the ancient Egyptian mud-brick hatcheries that incubated thousands of eggs without a hen; the broody hen's instinct; imprinting at hatch; sexing day-old chicks (vent vs. feather sexing).
source: Britannica; poultry-science incubation references; Egyptian hatchery history (Reaumur accounts)
framing_note: Scene-led: the ancient Egyptian mud-oven hatcheries warming thousands of eggs without a single hen. The 21-day number is constructed by the stem. No policy drift.

name: Barnyard Fowl: Guinea, Quail & Squab
scope: Guinea fowl (African, loud 'watchdog' alarm callers that eat ticks); Japanese quail (fast-maturing, farmed for tiny eggs and meat); pigeons raised for squab (the young dovecote pigeon, a medieval delicacy and the dovecote as a status symbol); ostrich and emu ratite farming for red meat and leather.
source: Britannica; The Livestock Conservancy; poultry-husbandry references
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the loud African fowl kept as a tick-eating alarm system' -> guinea fowl; 'the young dovecote pigeon served as a delicacy' -> squab. Named bird + role. No policy drift.

name: The Seven AKC Dog Groups
scope: The AKC's seven groups — Sporting, Hound, Working, Terrier, Toy, Non-Sporting, Herding — and the job each was bred for; how function (retrieve, scent-trail, guard, go-to-ground, lap, herd) defines the group; a signature breed per group; sighthound vs. scenthound within the Hound group.
source: American Kennel Club group definitions; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the group bred to go down burrows after vermin' → Terrier; 'the group bred to move sheep and cattle' → Herding. Function beats the label. No policy drift.

name: Herding & Sled Dogs
scope: Border Collie (top of Stanley Coren's intelligence ranking; herds by 'the eye'; Welsh/Northumbrian heritage); Australian Shepherd and Corgi as herders; Siberian Husky (Chukchi sled origin, double coat) and Alaskan Malamute (freight hauler); the herding 'outrun/lift/fetch' vocabulary; gee/haw sled commands.
source: AKC; Stanley Coren, The Intelligence of Dogs; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the breed that controls a flock with a hypnotic stare' → Border Collie; 'the freight-hauling Arctic breed heavier than the racing husky' → Malamute. Named breed + vivid job. No policy drift.

name: Working & Military Dogs
scope: German Shepherd (Max von Stephanitz, 1899; police/military/service versatility); Belgian Malinois (modern US military working dog — Cairo on the bin Laden raid; drive and bite work); Doberman, Rottweiler and Boxer as guard/working breeds; Newfoundland and Saint Bernard as rescue haulers; the schutzhund/IPO sport.
source: AKC; Britannica; military-working-dog program histories
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the breed founded by Max von Stephanitz in 1899' → German Shepherd; 'the breed that went on the bin Laden raid' → Malinois. Named breed + job/handler. No policy drift.

name: Popular & Purpose-Bred Dogs
scope: Labrador Retriever (most popular AKC breed for 30+ years until the French Bulldog took #1 in 2022); Golden Retriever; Dachshund (German 'badger dog', long body bred to enter setts); Beagle and Bloodhound (scent-trailing); the 'pit bull' terminology (a type, not one registry breed — American Pit Bull Terrier, American Staffordshire, Staffordshire Bull Terrier).
source: AKC registration statistics; Britannica; UKC/AKC breed standards
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the low German hound bred to squeeze into a badger's sett' → Dachshund. The Frenchie-overtakes-Lab 2022 fact is a memorable beat. Present 'pit bull' terminology factually (type not breed) without policy drift.

name: Brachycephalic Breeding & Welfare
scope: Flat-faced (brachycephalic) breeds — Bulldog, Pug, French Bulldog — and the health costs of extreme conformation: BOAS (brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome), overheating, birthing by C-section, eye and spine problems; how selection for an exaggerated 'cute' face imposed suffering; the welfare argument for moderating the standard toward a functional muzzle.
source: Royal Veterinary College BOAS research; UK Kennel Club Breed Watch; Britannica
framing_note: HUMANE-TREATMENT stance FIRM here: selecting for an extreme flat face that leaves a dog struggling to breathe is a welfare cost, and the case for moderating the standard is sound — state it plainly (not a neutral 'some say'). Scene-led on the snuffling, overheating flat-faced pup. No breed-ban policy drift.

name: Desert & Racing Horses
scope: Arabian (Bedouin desert origin; oldest documented breed; dished face, high tail carriage, one fewer rib/vertebra; foundation stock for many breeds); Thoroughbred (English 1600s; three founding sires — Byerley Turk, Darley Arabian, Godolphin Arabian — basis of flat racing); Quarter Horse (American; fastest over a quarter-mile sprint; cow-work + 'cow sense').
source: Britannica; The Jockey Club; American Quarter Horse Association; Arabian Horse Association
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the dish-faced desert horse behind nearly every modern breed' → Arabian; 'the sprinter unbeatable over a quarter-mile' → Quarter Horse. Named breed + signature trait. No policy drift.

name: Draft Giants & Feral Horses
scope: Clydesdale (Scottish draft; feathered legs; Budweiser hitch; ~1 tonne); Shire (English; among the tallest/heaviest horses; medieval war-horse lineage); Percheron and Belgian drafts; the Mustang (feral descendants of Spanish horses roaming the American West); the Przewalski's horse as the last truly wild horse; why draft breeds carried armored knights.
source: Britannica; American Shire Horse Association; Clydesdale Breeders USA
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the feather-legged Scottish giant of the Budweiser hitch' → Clydesdale; 'the last truly wild horse, never domesticated' → Przewalski's. Trait/association anchored. Keep Mustang about the ANIMAL, not land policy. No policy drift.

name: Ponies, Coat Breeds & Gaited Horses
scope: Appaloosa (spotted 'leopard' coat, selectively bred by the Nez Perce of the Palouse country); Andalusian/Lusitanian (Iberian baroque horses of classical dressage); Shetland and Welsh ponies; Tennessee Walker and the smooth four-beat gait; Friesian black beauty; coat-pattern genetics (leopard-complex, tobiano/overo).
source: Britannica; Appaloosa Horse Club; Nez Perce horse history; breed associations
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the spotted horse bred by the Nez Perce of the Palouse' → Appaloosa; 'the smooth-gaited breed you can ride without bouncing' → Tennessee Walker. Named breed + people/gait/coat. No policy drift.

name: Donkeys, Mules & Hinnies
scope: The donkey (domesticated from the African wild ass ~5,000 BP in Egypt/Nubia, the original pack animal); the mule (male donkey x female horse, hybrid vigor, sterile, sure-footed pack/plow animal) vs. the hinny (the reverse cross, rarer); why George Washington championed American mule breeding; the mammoth jack.
source: Britannica; American Donkey and Mule Society; Washington's Mount Vernon mule history
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the sure-footed sterile hybrid of a jack donkey and a mare' -> mule. The mule-vs-hinny cross direction is the load-bearing distinction. No policy drift.

name: USDA Egg Grades & Sizes
scope: USDA grades AA / A / B by air-cell size, albumen firmness and yolk centering (judged by candling); size classes by minimum weight per dozen (Jumbo 30oz → Extra Large → Large 24oz → Medium → Small → Peewee); why a fresh egg sinks and sits flat in water while an old one floats; how grade drives the fry-vs-scramble choice.
source: USDA AMS egg grading standards; American Egg Board
framing_note: Scene-led on candling and the float test: 'the top grade, tiny air cell, yolk standing tall' → AA. Stays scene-led (candling/float image), not a bare definition. Practical anchor: freshness you can judge. No policy drift.

name: Egg Labels & Shell Color
scope: Cage-free (uncaged but still indoors) vs. free-range (some outdoor access) vs. pasture-raised (most time outdoors) — what each label actually guarantees and where they blur; brown-vs-white shells is just hen breed, not nutrition; yolk color reflects feed (marigold/corn carotenoids), not quality; the myth that brown eggs are 'healthier'.
source: USDA labeling definitions; American Egg Board; Certified Humane label criteria
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the label that means uncaged but still under a roof' → cage-free. Debunk the brown-egg-is-healthier myth as the memorable beat. Humane-treatment context is fair to note; keep it about the label meaning, no legislative/policy drift.

name: The Five Freedoms (Brambell 1965)
scope: The 1965 Brambell Report (UK response to Ruth Harrison's 'Animal Machines') and the Farm Animal Welfare Council's Five Freedoms: freedom from hunger/thirst; from discomfort; from pain/injury/disease; to express normal behavior; from fear and distress; how this became the global welfare baseline; the newer 'Five Domains' successor that adds positive mental states.
source: Brambell Report 1965; UK Farm Animal Welfare Council; Mellor (2016) Five Domains
framing_note: HUMANE-TREATMENT stance FIRM: the Five Freedoms are real and matter — present them as a genuine, load-bearing standard, not one 'view'. Scene-led: Ruth Harrison's book that shamed a government into acting. No policy drift beyond the framework itself.

name: Welfare Certifications Compared
scope: Animal Welfare Approved / A Greener World (top marks on most metrics, pasture-required); Certified Humane (Humane Farm Animal Care non-profit, widely adopted); Global Animal Partnership's 5+1 step ratings sold at Whole Foods (Step 1 no-cage → Step 5+ animal-centered whole life); how these tiers differ and what a shopper's label actually promises; the difference between 'natural', 'organic' and welfare claims.
source: A Greener World; Humane Farm Animal Care; Global Animal Partnership standards
framing_note: HUMANE-TREATMENT stance FIRM but factual: present the certifications as real, meaningful tiers a buyer can trust to varying degrees. Scene-led: reading a carton's step-rating in the aisle. Compare programs, don't rank-shame; no policy drift.

name: Husbandry Practices: Marking & Castration
scope: Routine husbandry procedures and their welfare handling - ear-tagging and branding for ID, castration (banding vs. surgical) to make steers/wethers, dehorning/disbudding, tail-docking; why they're done (safety, meat quality, handling) and the modern push for pain relief and less-invasive methods; polled genetics as a way to skip dehorning entirely.
source: AVMA welfare guidelines on castration/dehorning; The Livestock Conservancy; Britannica
framing_note: HUMANE-TREATMENT stance FIRM: these procedures have real husbandry reasons AND doing them without pain relief is a welfare failure the field is right to be moving away from - state that plainly, note breeding polled cattle as the humane end-run. Scene-led on the disbudding iron / the banding. No legislative/policy drift.

name: CAFOs: Concerns & Tradeoffs
scope: Concentrated Animal Feeding Operations — the scale that made meat cheap; real concerns (manure lagoons and nutrient runoff, routine antibiotic use and resistance, confinement welfare, air quality, disease spread) set against the genuine cost / food-access tradeoff (industrial husbandry feeds billions affordably); why 'done well or poorly' matters more than the format alone.
source: EPA CAFO definitions; Pew Commission on Industrial Farm Animal Production; USDA data
framing_note: CONTESTED with a firm floor: cruelty is wrong (state that plainly), AND the cheap-food/access tradeoff is real — present the runoff/antibiotic/welfare concerns and the affordability case as a genuine debate, no verdict on the system itself. Scene-led on the lagoon and the feed bunk. No legislative/policy drift.

name: Salatin & Regenerative Grazing
scope: Joel Salatin's Polyface Farm (Virginia) — multispecies rotational grazing, 'salad-bar beef', chickens following cattle in eggmobiles to spread manure and eat larvae; the regenerative-ag toolkit (cover crops, integrated livestock, minimal tillage, biodiversity, soil-carbon building); mob/adaptive grazing that mimics wild herds; the mimic-the-herd logic.
source: Joel Salatin's writings / Polyface Farm; Michael Pollan, The Omnivore's Dilemma; Rodale Institute regenerative-ag material
framing_note: CONTESTED husbandry framed as a live debate: present regenerative grazing as a serious, well-argued approach (its soil and welfare case is real) while noting mainstream questions about scalability — no verdict either way. Scene-led on the eggmobile trailing the cattle. No policy drift.

name: Savory's Holistic Grazing Claim
scope: Allan Savory's Holistic Planned Grazing and his contested claim that intensive managed grazing can reverse desertification and sequester enough carbon to offset climate change; the widely-viewed TED talk; the peer-reviewed pushback (Briske et al.; Nordborg) finding the desertification-reversal and carbon claims unsupported at scale; supporters' rebuttals.
source: Allan Savory TED talk / Savory Institute; Briske et al. rangeland-science critiques; Nordborg (2016) review
framing_note: CONTESTED — both sides, no verdict, explicitly flag that Savory's desertification/carbon claims are disputed. Attribute the reversal claim to Savory and the null/critical findings to the rangeland scientists; let choices be the competing positions. Scene-led on the herd churning a bare patch back to grass. No policy drift.

name: Holstein Productivity vs. Longevity
scope: The modern Holstein produces roughly 4-5x the milk a 1950s cow did through relentless genetic selection; the tradeoff — shorter productive lifespan, more metabolic stress, lameness and mastitis, fewer lactations before culling; the debate over breeding for peak yield vs. cow longevity and welfare; the crossbreeding-for-fitness countermovement.
source: USDA/DHIA milk-yield trend data; dairy-science literature on cow longevity; Britannica
framing_note: CONTESTED tradeoff, both sides: the yield gains are real AND the longevity/welfare cost is real — present as a genuine breeding debate, no verdict. The 4-5x number is constructed by the stem. Scene-led on the record-yield cow culled after three lactations. No policy drift.

name: Heritage Breed Conservation
scope: The Livestock Conservancy and SVF Foundation preserving rare-breed genetic diversity (Mulefoot hog, Randall Lineback cattle, Gulf Coast sheep, Cotton Patch goose, Cayuga duck); why a narrow commercial gene pool is a resilience risk; the Conservancy's watch categories (Critical/Threatened/Recovering); frozen-genetics 'arks' as insurance against disease.
source: The Livestock Conservancy Conservation Priority List; SVF Foundation; FAO domestic-animal-diversity data
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the single-toed heritage hog the Conservancy lists as Critical' → Mulefoot. Frame conservation as protecting the ANIMAL's genetic diversity (a biology fact), not as policy/legislation. No policy drift.

name: Grass-Fed vs. Corn-Finished
scope: How finishing changes the meat — grass-fed carries higher omega-3 and beta-carotene (yellower fat) with leaner marbling; corn/grain-finishing builds intramuscular marbling faster and cheaper (feedlot economics); the omega-6:omega-3 ratio difference; the finishing-time and land-use tradeoff; why grass-finished takes longer and costs more.
source: Daley (2010) 'A review of fatty acid profiles... grass-fed and grain-fed beef'; USDA beef-quality data
framing_note: Scene-led + practical (butchery-relevant): 'the finishing that yellows the fat and raises omega-3s' → grass. Present as a real production/nutrition tradeoff (leaner vs. marbled, cost, time), not a moral verdict on either. No policy drift.

name: Feedlots, Rations & Silage
scope: The finishing feedlot and the total mixed ration; silage (fermented chopped corn/grass in a silo or bunker) as the winter feed that freed herds from seasonal grazing; hay vs. haylage; the rumen and why cattle can turn grass and grain byproducts humans can't eat into protein; growth-promotant and ionophore use (contested).
source: Britannica; USDA feed/silage references; ruminant-nutrition texts
framing_note: Scene-led: the silo of fermented corn that carries a herd through winter, and the rumen turning cellulose into steak. Present growth-promotant use factually as a contested efficiency practice, no verdict. Practical anchor. No policy drift.

name: Terroir of Meat: Pasture to Flavor
scope: How diet and life shape flavor a harvester tastes - acorn-finished Iberico's nutty fat, salt-marsh (pre-sale) lamb grazed on coastal samphire, alpine dairy from summer high-pasture flowers, the wild-forage 'gamey' note; the fat as the flavor library; why heritage-breed slow growth deposits different marbling; the maturity/age-at-slaughter effect.
source: McGee, On Food and Cooking; Britannica; pre-sale and dehesa references
framing_note: Scene-led + practical (this is exactly the harvester's payoff): 'the lamb grazed on coastal salt-marsh samphire, prized for its flavor' -> pre-sale. Present as production/flavor facts, no moral verdict on any system. No policy drift.

name: Falconry: Living Heritage
scope: Falconry inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list (2010, expanded 2016 to a joint nomination by 18+ countries); the hawk-hunting partnership; manning, imprinting and hooding the bird; jesses and the gauntlet; the practice's ancient Central-Asian roots and its living modern form; the medieval rank hierarchy of birds.
source: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list; Britannica 'falconry'
framing_note: Scene-led: the hooded hawk on a gauntleted fist, the world's most widely-shared heritage nomination. Named practice + the multinational listing are the hooks. No policy drift.

name: The Langstroth Hive Revolution
scope: Lorenzo Langstroth's 1851 discovery of 'bee space' — the ~3/8-inch (~1 cm) gap bees leave uncemented — and the movable-frame hive it enabled (patented 1852); why removable frames let a keeper inspect and harvest without destroying the colony; ~75% of hives worldwide still use his design; smoker and queen-excluder tools.
source: L. L. Langstroth (Wikipedia); Smithsonian 'the one-centimeter air gap'; National Inventors Hall of Fame
framing_note: Scene-led: the reverend measuring the exact gap bees refuse to fill, then lifting out a frame intact. The 3/8-inch 'bee space' is the load-bearing specific fact. No policy drift.

name: Colony Collapse Disorder
scope: Colony Collapse Disorder — first widely reported in 2006, workers abandoning a hive with queen and brood left behind; the multifactorial causes (Varroa destructor mite, neonicotinoid pesticides, viruses/Nosema, poor nutrition from monoculture); why no single cause explains it; managed-bee pollination stakes ($15B+ US crops); almond-pollination migration.
source: USDA ARS CCD reports; van Engelsdorp (2009) CCD studies; EPA neonicotinoid assessments
framing_note: Scene-led: a hive found empty but for the queen and unhatched brood. Present the multifactorial explanation (Varroa + pesticides + pathogens + nutrition), not a single-villain story. Note the neonicotinoid role as one contested factor among several. Keep it about the bees, no pesticide-ban policy drift.

name: Livestock Guardian Dogs
scope: Great Pyrenees, Anatolian Shepherd, Maremma, Kangal, Kuvasz — guardians that live inside the flock and drive off wolves and coyotes; the difference from herding dogs (guard vs. move); bonding with sheep from puppyhood so the dog identifies as flock; the Kangal's bite force and the spiked wolf-collar tradition; night-barking and perimeter patrol behavior.
source: The Livestock Conservancy; Britannica; USDA livestock-guardian-dog research
framing_note: Scene-led: 'the great white dog that beds down among the sheep and faces the wolf' → Great Pyrenees. The guardian-vs-herder distinction is the reveal. No policy drift.

name: Sled Dogs & the Iditarod
scope: The ~1,000-mile Anchorage-to-Nome Iditarod (founded 1973 by Joe Redington Sr.) commemorating the 1925 diphtheria serum run (Balto and Togo); sled-dog breeds (Alaskan Husky the working crossbreed, Siberian Husky, Malamute); gee/haw commands; the lead dog's role; team positions (wheel, swing, lead).
source: Iditarod Trail Committee history; Britannica; 1925 Nome serum-run record
framing_note: Scene-led: the 1925 serum relay racing diphtheria antitoxin to Nome, honored by today's race. Named race + the serum-run origin are the hooks. Keep it about the dogs. No policy drift.

name: Mongolian Horse Culture
scope: The stocky, hardy Mongolian horse (roughly one per person historically); Genghis Khan's mounted archers with 3-5 remounts each giving unmatched range; airag (fermented mare's milk) as staple; the horse as transport, weapon, food and drink in one animal; free-grazing herds still central to nomadic life; the Naadam horse race for children jockeys.
source: Britannica; Weatherford, Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World; Mongolian horse-culture ethnography
framing_note: Scene-led: the archer switching to a fresh remount at the gallop, sustained on fermented mare's milk. Named drink (airag) + the remount system are the memorable facts. No policy drift.

name: Guide, Detection & Service Animals
scope: Guide-dog training (first German school after WWI for blinded veterans; The Seeing Eye 1929, Morris Frank); medical-detection dogs (cancer, seizure-alert, diabetic-alert, COVID scent); the extraordinary canine nose (~300M receptors) put to work; the working ox/mule/donkey as draft animals; oxen yoked for plowing before tractors.
source: The Seeing Eye history; Medical Detection Dogs UK / Penn Vet; Britannica draft-animal history
framing_note: Scene-led: the dog that alerts to a coming seizure minutes before it strikes. Practical anchor on the nose (~300M receptors). Named milestone (Seeing Eye 1929). No policy drift.

name: Rabbits & Small-Stock Husbandry
scope: Domestic rabbit (from the European rabbit, domesticated by medieval French monks who raised laurices) for meat, fur (Rex velvet coat) and Angora wool; the doe's induced ovulation and rapid breeding; the New Zealand White and Flemish Giant meat breeds; cavies (guinea pigs) as Andean livestock (cuy).
source: The Livestock Conservancy; Britannica; medieval monastic rabbit-keeping history
framing_note: Scene-led: the medieval French monks who first bred rabbits in warrens for meat. Named origin + the induced-ovulation fact behind their fertility. No policy drift.

name: Salmon Aquaculture (Norway)
scope: Norway's invention of commercial Atlantic salmon net-pen farming in the 1970s, now the world's largest producer (~1.5M tons/year); the smolt-to-market cycle (freshwater then seawater pens); sea-lice and escapee-genetics concerns; feed conversion and the fishmeal/fish-oil question; why sheltered fjords suit the industry.
source: FAO aquaculture statistics; Norwegian Seafood Council; Marine Institute sea-lice research
framing_note: Scene-led: the fjord net-pens that made farmed salmon a global staple. Present sea-lice/escapee concerns factually alongside the production scale, no verdict. Named country + product. No policy drift.

name: Tilapia, Carp & Freshwater Farming
scope: Tilapia — among the most farmed fish globally, native to the Nile and one of the oldest aquaculture species (depicted in ~4,000-year-old Egyptian tomb art); hardy, fast-growing, low-trophic plant/algae feeder (the 'aquatic chicken'); mouthbrooding parental care; Chinese carp polyculture (the four famous carps) as the world's largest freshwater aquaculture tradition.
source: FAO aquaculture data; Britannica; Egyptian tomb depictions of tilapia ponds; Chinese carp-polyculture history
framing_note: Scene-led: the fish farmed in ancient Egyptian tomb paintings, now the world's 'aquatic chicken'. The 4,000-year Nile heritage is the wonder beat. No policy drift.

name: Oyster & Shellfish Farming
scope: Chesapeake Bay's eastern oyster crashed to <1% of historic abundance (overharvest + disease MSX/Dermo + habitat loss); restoration since the 1990s via reef-building and spat-on-shell; the oyster as a filter-feeder cleaning ~50 gallons/day; farming oysters on leases as both food and water-quality tool; mussel-rope and clam culture; merroir (place-flavor).
source: Chesapeake Bay Foundation; NOAA oyster-restoration reports; Britannica
framing_note: Scene-led: a single oyster filtering ~50 gallons a day, and a bay's reefs down to 1% of what they were. The filtration fact anchors why the animal matters. Keep it about the oyster's biology/restoration, not statute. No policy drift.

name: Shrimp Farms & Mangroves
scope: Southeast Asian coastal shrimp ponds (whiteleg Litopenaeus vannamei and black tiger prawn) cleared an estimated ~38% of the region's mangrove forests between 1980 and 2000; the tradeoff — cheap protein and coastal livelihoods vs. lost storm-buffering nursery habitat; the contested practice; the shift toward certified/closed-recirculating farming.
source: FAO; Valiela (2001) mangrove-loss estimates; Global Aquaculture Alliance / ASC certification
framing_note: CONTESTED practice — note it explicitly and even-handedly: the mangrove destruction is real AND the livelihood/protein case is real; present as a debate, no verdict. Scene-led on the pond carved from the mangrove. Keep it about the practice and the habitat, no legislative/policy drift.
